title: The painted porch
hook: Zeno teaches in a public colonnade, and the school takes its name from the porch

segments.voice: Yesterday: Crates, the Cynic who cracked a pot of soup and told a shy Zeno that embarrassment isn't harm.
screen: `CRATES — NOTHING TERRIBLE HAS HAPPENED TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Where do you teach, when you have no money, no building, no school? Around the year three hundred BCE, after years learning from Crates and other teachers in Athens, that was Zeno's problem. He picked the middle of the city. Not behind a wall, not in a private garden. On the edge of the marketplace, the agora, where everyone walked past all day long.
screen: `NO MONEY, NO BUILDING.` → `THE MIDDLE OF THE CITY.` → `THE EDGE OF THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: He taught under a stoa: a colonnade, a long roof held up by a row of columns, open on one side, where people could get out of the sun or the rain. Athens had several. Zeno's was the Stoa Poikile, the painted porch, because its walls held great paintings by famous artists, including a scene of the Battle of Marathon, the day Athens fought off a Persian invasion. Picture it. Merchants shouting in the market. People sheltering from the heat. Travelers staring at the paintings. And a thin, serious man from Cyprus walking up and down between the columns, talking, while anyone who wanted to could stop and listen. Diogenes Laërtius says his followers were first called Zenonians, after him. But the name that stuck was the place: people who met at the porch. The Stoics. Other schools in Athens met in other kinds of places. Plato's Academy was in a grove outside the city walls. Epicurus gathered his friends in a private garden. Each place suited its school, and the Stoics' fit is almost too good. Their whole teaching was about living well in the middle of ordinary life: the market, the law court, the family, the army. Not by escaping the world, but in it. Two thousand three hundred years later, the name of a building is still the name of a way of life. Every time someone says stoic, they're pointing, without knowing it, at a painted porch in the middle of a crowd.
screen: `A LONG ROOF ON A ROW OF COLUMNS.` · `PAINTINGS OF MARATHON.` · `ZENONIANS, THEN STOICS.` · `LIVING WELL IN THE MIDDLE OF LIFE.` · then, large: `WISDOM IN THE OPEN.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are, a bus, a cafe, a park, or at home picturing a busy street you know, sit with your eyes open or half closed. Let the noise and the movement go on around you, people passing, sounds coming and going; you don't have to escape it to be steady. Breathe in the middle of it, the way Zeno taught in the middle of the market.
Stoa. A porch with columns, open to the street, and the place that gave the Stoics their name.
Your line: wisdom in the open. Not behind a wall, but in the middle of the crowd. See you at the wells tomorrow.

howItsDone: Stoicism has always been practiced in ordinary life rather than apart from it: its followers aim to be steady and just in public roles, at work and in the family.

original.note: Greek, stoa poikilē: the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught, and the source of the words Stoic and stoic.
